deep.reconstruction:
The page has no mathematics: no formulas, derivations or computations. It is the title page and opening of Riemann's epistemological programme, 'Versuch einer Lehre von den Grundbegriffen der Mathematik und Physik als Grundlage für die Naturerklärung' ('Attempt at a theory of the basic concepts of mathematics and physics as a foundation for explaining nature'). The argument runs as follows.

(1) Definition. Natural science is the attempt to grasp nature through precise concepts ('genaue Begriffe', underlined).

(2) Role of a conceptual system. At each moment it completes our perceptions. It also predetermines future perceptions, as necessary or, where the system is incomplete, as probable. It fixes what is possible, and so what is necessary, meaning its opposite is impossible. If the concepts are precise enough, the degree of possibility (the probability) of each possible event can be determined mathematically.

(3) Confirmation and revision. When the necessary or probable event occurs, the system is confirmed, and our trust in it rests on such confirmation by experience. When something impossible or improbable by the system's lights occurs, the task arises of supplementing or reworking the system until the observation is no longer impossible or improbable. That supplement or correction is the 'Erklärung' (explanation) of the unexpected perception. Through this process our grasp of nature becomes ever more complete and correct, and reaches ever further behind the surface of phenomena.

(4) Historical support. The history of the explanatory sciences shows that this is in fact how knowledge advances. Present conceptual systems arose by gradual transformation of older ones, and every change of explanation traces back to contradictions or improbabilities found in the older ones. So the formation of new concepts, as far as we can observe it, happens by this process.

(5) Appeal to Herbart, against Kant. Herbart is said to have shown that even the concepts we inherit unnoticed with language can all be derived from this same source, insofar as they are more than mere forms of combining simple sensory representations. They therefore need not be traced, as Kant's categories are, to a constitution of the soul prior to all experience. Establishing this origin in the apprehension of experience matters because only so can the concepts' meaning be fixed adequately for natural science. Riemann declines to set out the psychological process of concept formation in detail.

In modern terms this is a fallibilist, quasi-Bayesian and hypothetico-deductive account of scientific concept formation. Probability is treated as a graded modality between necessity and impossibility, and theory change is driven by surprise, i.e. improbable observations.

results.what: Epistemological programme: natural science as a system of precise concepts that predicts events as necessary or probable (with mathematically determinable probabilities) and is revised when improbable events occur; 'explanation' = the revision of the conceptual system.
results.modern_name: Fallibilist / hypothetico-deductive account of theory change, with a proto-Bayesian, probabilistic notion of confirmation
results.usually_credited_to: Various authors (Whewell, Herschel, later Peirce and Popper); Riemann's version is a known text

results.what: Herbartian empiricist derivation of fundamental concepts, explicitly against Kant's a priori categories
results.modern_name: Herbartian psychology and epistemology as applied to the foundations of physics
results.usually_credited_to: J. F. Herbart; Riemann's Herbartian stance is well documented (Scholz, Ferreirós and others)

deep.surprise_reason: This is the well-known opening of Riemann's 'Fragmente philosophischen Inhalts' (the Naturphilosophie fragments). Dedekind and Weber published it in the Gesammelte Werke (1876), and historians such as E. Scholz and J. Ferreirós have discussed it extensively, including its Herbartian background. The page contains no mathematics.
transcription_corrections: Several words or phrases appear underlined in the manuscript (from my reading of the image): 'genaue Begriffe', 'was' in 'was (noch) möglich', 'Proceß' at the end of the second paragraph, 'Herbart', 'die' in 'auch die zur Weltauffassung', and the passage 'nur dadurch ihre Bedeutung in einer für die Naturwissenschaft genügenden Weise festgestellt werden kann'.
The parenthetical '(noch)' after 'was' is uncertain in the image. The published Werke text reads simply 'was möglich ist'.

The interlinear insertion near 'in der Auffassung' is only partly legible. It appears to read roughly 'der Erfahrung (oder sinnlichen Wahrnehmung)', replacing a struck-through word. The struck reading 'des Gegebenen' is doubtful.
The top-right archival note 'Riemann 18' and the circled folio number '86' are archival markings, not Riemann's text.
